title: Solving Linear Equations and Inequalities
bigQuestion: How do you know that the number you found is really the answer, and not just a number?

story.title: The Formula on the Back of the Fertilizer Bag
story.kicker: A community garden, a 20-pound bag, and one line of small print that turns out to be algebra.
paragraphs: Jasmine volunteers on Saturdays at a community garden on the South Side of Chicago. In April the garden coordinator hands her a 20-pound bag of fertilizer and points at the raised beds. "Spread the right amount," she says, "too little does nothing and too much burns the roots." Jasmine flips the bag over. On the back, in small print, is one sentence: apply 3 pounds for every 1,000 square feet.

That sentence is a formula in disguise. Jasmine paces off the main bed: 40 feet by 60 feet. She multiplies to get the area, 40 × 60 = 2,400 square feet. Then she reasons: 2,400 is 2.4 groups of 1,000, so she needs 2.4 × 3 = 7.2 pounds. She writes the rule with letters so she never has to think it through again: pounds = 0.003 × area, because 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.003. Check: 0.003 × 2,400 = 7.2. It matches.

Now the coordinator asks the question backwards. "We have 20 pounds. How much ground can one bag cover?" This time the pounds are known and the area is the mystery. Jasmine writes 20 = 0.003 × A and asks herself what undoes multiplying by 0.003. Dividing by 0.003 does. So A = 20 ÷ 0.003, which is about 6,667 square feet. One bag covers the main bed almost three times over.

By the end of the morning Jasmine has used the same formula four different ways: forward, backward, for a bed shaped like an L, and to decide whether one bag is enough for the whole season. Every time, she does one thing: she treats the equation as a sentence that must stay true, and she does the same thing to both sides. That single habit is what this chapter is about.
story.think: The bag says 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet. Jasmine's friend says a 30-by-30-foot bed needs 9 pounds. Is he right? Explain how you would check without a calculator.

lessons.title: True, False or Open
lessons.mainIdea: An equation is a statement that can be true or false, and a solution is a value that makes it true.
reading: Look at three sentences: 3 + 4 = 7, 3 + 4 = 8, and x + 4 = 7. The first is true. The second is false. The third is neither, because it has a blank in it. A sentence with a variable is called an *open sentence*: it becomes true or false only after you fill in a number. Fill in 3 and you get 3 + 4 = 7, true. Fill in 5 and you get 5 + 4 = 7, false. So an *equation* is not a command to "do something." It is a claim that two sides are equal, and your job is to find out when that claim holds.

A number that makes the equation true is a *solution*. To test a number, you *substitute* it for the variable and simplify both sides. Is 5 a solution of 2x − 3 = 7? Substitute: 2(5) − 3 = 10 − 3 = 7. The left side is 7, the right side is 7, so yes. Is 4 a solution? 2(4) − 3 = 8 − 3 = 5, and 5 is not 7, so no. This testing step is the most important habit in algebra, because it works no matter how you found the number.

Students sometimes decide a number is a solution because it "looks right" or because it appeared in the problem. The test does not care about looks. For 3x + 2 = 17, the number 17 is in the problem, but 3(17) + 2 = 53, not 17. The number 5 is not in the problem, but 3(5) + 2 = 17, so 5 is the solution. Always substitute and compare the two sides before you trust an answer.

words.d: a statement that two expressions are equal, like 2x − 3 = 7
a statement with a variable that is true or false only after a number is put in
a value of the variable that makes the equation true
replace the variable with a number so you can simplify and check

look.title: Test Three Numbers
look.text: The equation is 3x + 2 = 17. Try x = 4: 3(4) + 2 = 14, not 17. Try x = 5: 3(5) + 2 = 17, true. Try x = 6: 3(6) + 2 = 20, not 17. Only one of the three works.
look.prompt: Now test 4, 5 and 6 in 4x − 1 = 19. Which one is the solution, and how do you know?

check.q: Which value is a solution of 4x − 6 = 18?
check.why: 4(6) − 6 = 24 − 6 = 18, so 6 makes both sides equal. The others give 6, 14 and 26.

check.q: What does it mean for a number to be a solution of an equation?
choices: Substituting it makes both sides equal
It appears somewhere in the equation
It is the largest number that fits
It makes the left side equal zero
check.why: A solution makes the equation a true statement: after substituting, the left side and right side simplify to the same number.

check.q: Is 7 a solution of 2x + 5 = 19?
choices: No, because 7 is not in the equation
check.why: Substitute 7: 2(7) + 5 = 14 + 5 = 19, which equals the right side, so 7 is a solution.

lessons.title: Keeping the Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other side, and the statement stays true.
reading: Picture a balance scale that is level. Add 2 pounds to the left pan only and it tips. Add 2 pounds to both pans and it stays level. An equation works the same way. The *properties of equality* say you can add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number and the new equation has the same solution as the old one. That is the whole toolkit for solving. You use it to *isolate* the variable, which means getting it alone on one side.

Solve 3x + 7 = 22. The variable is wrapped in two operations: multiplied by 3, then 7 is added. Undo them in reverse order using *inverse operations*. First subtract 7 from both sides: 3x + 7 − 7 = 22 − 7, so 3x = 15. Then divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Check by substituting: 3(5) + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22. True. Notice the *coefficient* 3 was handled last, because it was applied to x first.

One more: x/4 − 2 = 3. Add 2 to both sides: x/4 = 5. Multiply both sides by 4: x = 20. Check: 20/4 − 2 = 5 − 2 = 3. The most common mistake is doing the step on one side only, writing 3x = 22 − 7 but then forgetting the 7 was also on the left. Another is dividing only one term, turning 3x + 7 = 22 into x + 7 = 22/3. Every operation touches the whole of both sides.

words.d: the rules that let you add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides of an equation by the same number
get the variable alone on one side of the equation
operations that undo each other, like adding 7 and subtracting 7
the number multiplying a variable, like the 3 in 3x

look.title: The Text Message Bill
look.text: A phone plan costs $45 a month plus $0.10 for each text over the limit. One month the bill is $52.50. Let t be the number of extra texts: 45 + 0.10t = 52.50. Subtract 45 from both sides: 0.10t = 7.50. Divide both sides by 0.10: t = 75. Check: 45 + 0.10(75) = 45 + 7.50 = 52.50.
look.prompt: The next month's bill is $61.20. Set up the same kind of equation and find the number of extra texts.

check.q: Solve 5x − 8 = 27.
check.why: Add 8 to both sides: 5x = 35. Divide by 5: x = 7. Check: 5(7) − 8 = 27. Forgetting to divide gives 35.

check.q: Solve x/3 + 4 = 10.
check.why: Subtract 4: x/3 = 6. Multiply by 3: x = 18. Check: 18/3 + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10. Adding 4 instead of subtracting it gives 14 × 3 = 42, a common slip.

check.q: What is the best first step to solve 2x + 9 = 25?
choices: Subtract 9 from the left side only
check.why: Undo the addition first: subtracting 9 from both sides gives 2x = 16, then dividing gives x = 8. Dividing first would force you to divide the 9 too.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Equations with Reasons
lessons.mainIdea: Simplify each side first, then collect the variable on one side, and name the reason for every step.
reading: Some equations have parentheses, several terms, and variables on both sides. Solve 4(x − 3) + 2x = 3x + 6. Start by cleaning up each side. The *distributive property* turns 4(x − 3) into 4x − 12, because the 4 multiplies both the x and the 3. Now the left side is 4x − 12 + 2x. Combine the *like terms* 4x and 2x to get 6x − 12. The equation is now 6x − 12 = 3x + 6.

Next, get all the x terms on one side. Subtract 3x from both sides: 3x − 12 = 6. Add 12 to both sides: 3x = 18. Divide both sides by 3: x = 6. Check in the original equation: 4(6 − 3) + 2(6) = 4(3) + 12 = 24, and 3(6) + 6 = 24. Both sides are 24, so x = 6 is correct. Writing the reason next to each step is called *justifying* it: distributive property, combine like terms, subtraction property of equality, addition property, division property.

Two mistakes cause most wrong answers here. The first is distributing to only the first term, writing 4(x − 3) as 4x − 3. Try it with numbers: 4(5 − 3) = 8, but 4(5) − 3 = 17, so those are not the same. The second is moving a term across the equals sign without changing its sign. Subtracting 3x from the right side means subtracting 3x from the left side too. Justifying each step forces you to notice both errors.

words.d: a(b + c) = ab + ac; the number outside multiplies every term inside
terms with the same variable part, such as 4x and 2x, which can be combined
state the property or rule that makes a step legal

look.title: Every Step, One Reason
look.text: Solve 5(2x + 1) − 3x = 2x + 30. Distribute: 10x + 5 − 3x = 2x + 30. Combine like terms: 7x + 5 = 2x + 30. Subtract 2x from both sides: 5x + 5 = 30. Subtract 5: 5x = 25. Divide by 5: x = 5. Check: 5(11) − 15 = 40 and 2(5) + 30 = 40.
look.prompt: Solve 3(x + 4) − x = x + 20 the same way, writing the reason beside each line. What do you get, and does it check?

check.why: Distribute: 3x + 6 = 2x + 11. Subtract 2x: x + 6 = 11. Subtract 6: x = 5. Writing 3x + 2 instead of 3x + 6 gives the wrong answer 9.

check.q: Which property justifies going from 2x + 6 = 14 to 2x = 8?
check.why: Six was subtracted from both sides, which the subtraction property of equality allows without changing the solution.

check.q: Solve 7x − 4 = 3x + 20.
check.why: Subtract 3x: 4x − 4 = 20. Add 4: 4x = 24. Divide: x = 6. Check: 7(6) − 4 = 38 and 3(6) + 20 = 38. Adding 3x instead of subtracting gives 24/10 = 2.4.

lessons.title: Rearranging a Formula
lessons.mainIdea: A formula with several letters is solved the same way as any equation: undo operations until the letter you want stands alone.
reading: The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2l + 2w. Usually you know the length and width and want P. But a fence builder often knows the total fencing and the length, and needs the width. A formula with more than one letter is a *literal equation*, and you can *solve for* any letter in it. Treat every other letter as if it were a known number.

Try it with numbers first. If P = 50 and l = 15, then 50 = 2(15) + 2w, so 50 = 30 + 2w. Subtract 30 from both sides: 20 = 2w. Divide by 2: w = 10. Now do the identical steps with letters. Start with P = 2l + 2w. Subtract 2l from both sides: P − 2l = 2w. Divide both sides by 2: w = (P − 2l)/2. Plug in P = 50 and l = 15 to see it give the same 10. The letter version is a new *formula* you can reuse for any fence.

Jasmine's fertilizer rule was pounds = 0.003 × A. To solve for A, divide both sides by 0.003: A = pounds/0.003. Six pounds covers 6/0.003 = 2,000 square feet. The classic error in rearranging is dividing only part of one side. From P − 2l = 2w, some students write w = P − 2l/2, which divides only the 2l. Parentheses matter: the whole expression P − 2l is divided by 2.

words.d: an equation with two or more letters, such as P = 2l + 2w
a rule written as an equation that relates quantities, like A = lw
rearrange an equation so a chosen variable is alone on one side

look.title: Distance, Rate and Time
look.text: The distance formula is d = rt. A CTA bus averaging 30 miles per hour that needs to cover 45 miles: 45 = 30t. Divide both sides by 30: t = 1.5 hours. In letters, dividing both sides of d = rt by r gives t = d/r. The same rearrangement works for a car, a walker or a train.
look.prompt: Solve d = rt for r. Then use your formula to find the speed of a runner who covers 12 miles in 1.5 hours.

check.q: Solve A = lw for w.
check.why: The width is multiplied by l, so divide both sides by l: w = A/l. For example, a 24-square-foot rug 6 feet long is 24/6 = 4 feet wide.

check.q: Solve y = mx + b for x.
check.why: Subtract b from both sides: y − b = mx. Divide both sides by m: x = (y − b)/m. The whole difference y − b is divided by m.

check.q: Using P = 2l + 2w with P = 36 and l = 10, what is w?
check.why: 36 = 20 + 2w, so 2w = 16 and w = 8. Check: 2(10) + 2(8) = 36. Forgetting to divide by 2 gives 16.

lessons.title: Temperature and Other Conversions
lessons.mainIdea: A conversion formula can be run in either direction once you solve it for the other variable.
reading: Weather in Chicago is reported in degrees *Fahrenheit*, but science class and most of the world use *Celsius*. The two scales are linked by F = (9/5)C + 32. Water freezes at 0 °C, and the formula gives (9/5)(0) + 32 = 32 °F. Water boils at 100 °C: (9/5)(100) + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212 °F. A warm 25 °C day becomes (9/5)(25) + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77 °F.

To go the other way, solve for C. Start with F = (9/5)C + 32. Subtract 32 from both sides: F − 32 = (9/5)C. Multiply both sides by 5/9, which undoes multiplying by 9/5: C = (5/9)(F − 32). Test it on a hot summer afternoon of 86 °F: 86 − 32 = 54, and (5/9)(54) = 30, so 86 °F is 30 °C. A cold January morning of −4 °F: −4 − 32 = −36, and (5/9)(−36) = −20, so −4 °F is −20 °C. Both formulas are *equivalent*; they describe the same relationship.

The order of operations trap here is subtracting 32 after multiplying. (5/9)(86) − 32 = 47.8 − 32 = 15.8, which is wrong. The 32 is added last in the forward formula, so it must be removed first when going backward. Whenever you rearrange a formula, test your new version with one pair of values you already trust, such as 0 °C and 32 °F.

words.d: the temperature scale used in U.S. weather reports; water freezes at 32 °F
the temperature scale used in science; water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
two equations or formulas that describe exactly the same relationship

look.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
look.cite: computed from the standard formula F = (9/5)C + 32
look.prompt: Each 10 °C step adds the same number of °F. What is that number, and where does it come from in the formula?

check.q: Convert 50 °F to Celsius.
check.why: 50 − 32 = 18, and (5/9)(18) = 10. Stopping after subtracting gives 18; using the forward formula gives 122.

check.q: Convert 15 °C to Fahrenheit.
check.why: (9/5)(15) = 27, then 27 + 32 = 59. Forgetting to multiply gives 47; forgetting to add 32 gives 27.

check.q: Which is F = (9/5)C + 32 correctly solved for C?
check.why: Subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5/9. Check with 212 °F: (5/9)(180) = 100 °C, the boiling point.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Equations
lessons.mainIdea: An absolute value equation usually has two solutions, one on each side of the center point.
reading: The *absolute value* of a number is its *distance* from zero on the number line, ignoring direction. So |5| = 5 and |−5| = 5. That means the equation |x| = 5 has two solutions, 5 and −5, because two numbers sit five units from zero. The equation |x − 3| = 5 asks which numbers are 5 units from 3. Split it into two ordinary equations: x − 3 = 5 gives x = 8, and x − 3 = −5 gives x = −2. Check: |8 − 3| = 5 and |−2 − 3| = |−5| = 5.

If the absolute value is not alone, isolate it first. Solve 3|x| + 2 = 14. Subtract 2: 3|x| = 12. Divide by 3: |x| = 4, so x = 4 or x = −4. Now try |2x + 1| = 7. Case one: 2x + 1 = 7, so 2x = 6 and x = 3. Case two: 2x + 1 = −7, so 2x = −8 and x = −4. Check the second: |2(−4) + 1| = |−7| = 7. Both work.

A distance can never be negative, so |x| + 5 = 2 has no solution at all: it would need |x| = −3. Absolute value shows up in manufacturing as *tolerance*. A part must measure 50 millimeters, give or take 0.2 millimeters. The acceptable extremes solve |m − 50| = 0.2, giving m = 50.2 and m = 49.8. The common mistake is forgetting the second case and reporting only the positive answer.

words.d: the distance of a number from zero, written |x|; it is never negative
how far apart two numbers are on the number line, always zero or positive
how far a measurement may be from its target and still be accepted

look.title: Five Units from Seven
look.text: |x − 7| = 3 asks for the numbers that are 3 units away from 7. Going up: x − 7 = 3, so x = 10. Going down: x − 7 = −3, so x = 4. On a number line, 4 and 10 sit on either side of 7, each 3 steps away.
look.prompt: Write an absolute value equation whose solutions are 2 and 12. What is the center, and what is the distance?

check.q: What are the solutions of |x + 2| = 6?
check.why: x + 2 = 6 gives x = 4; x + 2 = −6 gives x = −8. Check: |−8 + 2| = |−6| = 6. Dropping the second case gives only 4.

check.q: How many solutions does |x| + 5 = 2 have?
check.why: Subtracting 5 gives |x| = −3. A distance cannot be negative, so no number works.

check.q: Solve |3x − 6| = 12.

lessons.title: Inequalities Show a Range
lessons.mainIdea: An inequality is solved like an equation, but its solution is a whole range of numbers, shown on a number line.
reading: An *inequality* compares two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥ instead of an equals sign. The statement x + 4 > 9 is true for x = 6, x = 10, x = 5.5 and infinitely many other values. All of those values together form the *solution set*. To find it, use the same balancing moves as with equations. Subtract 4 from both sides: x > 5. Every number greater than 5 works, and 5 itself does not.

Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 11. Add 3 to both sides: 2x ≤ 14. Divide by 2: x ≤ 7. Check with one number inside the range, say x = 0: 2(0) − 3 = −3, and −3 ≤ 11 is true. Check one number outside, say x = 10: 2(10) − 3 = 17, and 17 ≤ 11 is false. Checking both an inside and an outside value catches a wrong direction.

Draw the solution on a *number line*. The *boundary* number, 7, gets a closed dot because ≤ includes it, and an arrow points left toward all smaller numbers. For x > 5 the boundary 5 gets an open circle, because 5 is not included, and the arrow points right. The picture is the answer; a single number is not.

words.d: a statement comparing two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥
every value that makes the inequality true
a line with numbers in order, used to picture a solution set
the number where the solution set starts or stops

look.title: How Many Rides
look.text: You load $20 onto a transit card. Each ride costs $2.50. The number of rides r must satisfy 2.50r ≤ 20. Divide both sides by 2.50: r ≤ 8. You can take up to 8 rides. The solution set is the whole numbers from 0 to 8, because you cannot take part of a ride.
look.prompt: Suppose the card already has $4.25 on it before you load $20. Write and solve the new inequality.

check.q: Solve 3x + 5 < 20.
check.why: Subtract 5: 3x < 15. Divide by 3: x < 5. Check x = 0: 5 < 20 is true. Forgetting to divide gives x < 15.

check.q: Which value is in the solution set of x − 4 ≥ 2?
check.why: Adding 4 gives x ≥ 6, and 6 is included because of the ≥. Check: 6 − 4 = 2, and 2 ≥ 2 is true.

check.q: How is x ≤ 7 drawn on a number line?
choices: Open circle at 7, arrow to the right
Closed dot at 7, arrow to the left
Closed dot at 7, arrow to the right
Open circle at 7, arrow to the left
check.why: The ≤ includes 7, so the dot is closed, and the solutions are smaller than 7, so the arrow points left.

lessons.title: When the Sign Flips
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
reading: Start with a true statement: 2 < 5. Multiply both sides by −1. You get −2 and −5, and on the number line −2 is to the right of −5, so −2 > −5. The direction changed. Multiplying or dividing by a *negative coefficient* flips every number to the other side of zero and swaps the order. So the rule: whenever you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, *reverse* the sign.

Solve −3x + 4 ≥ 19. Subtract 4 from both sides: −3x ≥ 15. Now divide both sides by −3 and reverse the sign: x ≤ −5. Check with x = −6: −3(−6) + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22, and 22 ≥ 19 is true. Check with x = 0: 0 + 4 = 4, and 4 ≥ 19 is false. The inside value works and the outside value fails, so x ≤ −5 is right.

You can avoid the flip entirely by moving the variable to the other side. From −3x + 4 ≥ 19, add 3x to both sides: 4 ≥ 19 + 3x. Subtract 19: −15 ≥ 3x. Divide by positive 3: −5 ≥ x, which is the same *equivalent inequality* x ≤ −5. The common mistake is flipping at the wrong moment, such as when subtracting a negative number. Adding and subtracting never flip the sign; only multiplying or dividing by a negative does.

words.d: a variable multiplied by a negative number, like −3x
switch < to > or ≤ to ≥ (and back)
an inequality with exactly the same solution set as another

look.title: Two Roads, Same Answer
look.text: Solve 8 − 2x > 14. Road one: subtract 8 to get −2x > 6, then divide by −2 and flip: x < −3. Road two: add 2x to both sides to get 8 > 14 + 2x, subtract 14 to get −6 > 2x, divide by 2: −3 > x, which is x < −3. Check x = −4: 8 − 2(−4) = 16 > 14. True.
look.prompt: Solve 5 − 3x ≤ 20 both ways. Do you get the same answer? Which road do you prefer, and why?

check.q: Solve −4x < 12.
check.why: Divide both sides by −4 and reverse the sign: x > −3. Check x = 0: 0 < 12 is true, so 0 must be in the set.

check.q: Solve 5 − x ≥ 2.
check.why: Subtract 5: −x ≥ −3. Multiply by −1 and flip: x ≤ 3. Check x = 0: 5 ≥ 2 is true.

check.q: Which step requires reversing the inequality sign?
check.why: Only multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign. Adding or subtracting any number, positive or negative, does not.

lessons.title: Compound Inequalities
lessons.mainIdea: A compound inequality joins two conditions with 'and' or 'or', and you solve every part at once.
reading: A refrigerator should stay between 34 °F and 40 °F. That is two conditions at once: T ≥ 34 and T ≤ 40. Written as one *compound inequality*, it is 34 ≤ T ≤ 40. The solution is the *intersection*, the numbers that satisfy both parts, which forms an *interval* on the number line from 34 to 40 with closed dots at both ends.

Solve −2 < x + 3 ≤ 6. There are three parts, and whatever you do must be done to all three. Subtract 3 from every part: −5 < x ≤ 3. The solution is every number greater than −5 and at most 3. Check x = 0, which is inside: −2 < 3 ≤ 6, true. Check x = 5, outside: −2 < 8 ≤ 6 is false because 8 is not ≤ 6. A frequent error is subtracting 3 from only the middle and the right, leaving −2 unchanged.

An 'or' inequality is different. Solve 2x − 1 < −7 or 3x + 2 > 11. Handle each separately: 2x < −6 gives x < −3, and 3x > 9 gives x > 3. The solution is the *union*: x < −3 or x > 3, two arrows pointing away from each other with a gap between −3 and 3. Numbers like 0 are not solutions. With 'and' you keep only what both parts share; with 'or' you keep everything either part allows.

words.d: two inequalities joined by 'and' or 'or'
the values that satisfy both parts of an 'and' inequality
the values that satisfy at least one part of an 'or' inequality
a stretch of the number line between two boundaries

look.title: Three Parts at Once
look.text: Solve 1 ≤ 2x − 3 ≤ 9. Add 3 to all three parts: 4 ≤ 2x ≤ 12. Divide all three parts by 2: 2 ≤ x ≤ 6. Check the middle value x = 4: 2(4) − 3 = 5, and 1 ≤ 5 ≤ 9 is true. Check x = 7: 2(7) − 3 = 11, and 11 ≤ 9 is false.
look.prompt: Solve −4 < 3x + 2 < 14. Then name one whole number that is a solution and one that is not.

check.why: Subtract 2 from all three parts: −3 ≤ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ≤ x < 3. Leaving out the division gives −3 ≤ x < 9.

check.q: Which number satisfies x < −2 or x > 4?
check.why: −5 is less than −2, so it satisfies the first part. 0 and 3 sit in the gap, and 4 is not greater than 4.

check.q: How is 'x ≥ 3 and x ≤ 8' written as one inequality?
check.why: Both conditions hold at once, so x sits between 3 and 8 including both ends: 3 ≤ x ≤ 8.

lessons.title: Writing Equations from Situations
lessons.mainIdea: To model a situation, define a variable, translate the words into an equation, solve it, and say what the number means.
reading: A gym charges $25 to join and $15 per month. Someone has paid $130 in total. How many months have they been a member? A *model* is an equation that captures the situation. First *define the variable*: let m be the number of months. The join fee is paid once and the monthly fee is paid m times, so 25 + 15m = 130. Subtract 25: 15m = 105. Divide by 15: m = 7. Finally *interpret*: they have been a member for 7 months. Check: 25 + 15(7) = 25 + 105 = 130.

Number puzzles use the same steps. Three consecutive integers add up to 48. Let n be the smallest. The next two are n + 1 and n + 2. The equation is n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 48, which simplifies to 3n + 3 = 48. Subtract 3: 3n = 45. Divide: n = 15. The integers are 15, 16 and 17, and 15 + 16 + 17 = 48.

Watch the key phrases. 'Twice a number decreased by 7' is 2n − 7, not 2(n − 7); the decrease happens after the doubling. 'Seven less than a number' is n − 7, not 7 − n. If the wording is unclear, plug in an easy number and see which expression matches what the sentence says. Then, after solving, always read your answer back into the story to see whether it makes sense.

words.d: an equation or inequality that represents a real situation
state in words exactly what the letter stands for, including units
explain what the solved number means in the original situation

look.title: Tickets Plus a Fee
look.text: Four concert tickets plus a single $12 service fee cost $172 in total. Let t be the price of one ticket: 4t + 12 = 172. Subtract 12: 4t = 160. Divide by 4: t = 40. Each ticket is $40. Check: 4(40) + 12 = 172.
look.prompt: Six tickets to a different show plus a $15 fee cost $195. Write the equation, solve it and state the ticket price.

check.q: A gym charges $25 to join and $15 per month. A member has paid $175. How many months is that?
Which equation says 'twice a number decreased by 7 is 19'?
check.why: Double the number first, then subtract 7: 2n − 7 = 19. Solving gives n = 13, and 2(13) − 7 = 19.

check.q: Two consecutive even integers add to 54. What are they?
check.why: Let n be the first: n + (n + 2) = 54, so 2n = 52 and n = 26. The integers are 26 and 28, and 26 + 28 = 54.

lessons.title: Limits Become Inequalities
lessons.mainIdea: Words like 'at most', 'at least' and 'no more than' signal an inequality, and the answer is a range that may need rounding.
reading: A freight elevator is rated for 2,000 pounds. A cart weighing 180 pounds is already inside, and each worker weighs about 150 pounds. How many workers can ride? The limit is a *constraint*, and 'rated for' means the total must be *at most* 2,000. Let p be the number of workers: 180 + 150p ≤ 2000. Subtract 180: 150p ≤ 1820. Divide by 150: p ≤ 12.13. You cannot have 0.13 of a person, so at most 12 workers can ride. Rounding up to 13 would break the limit: 180 + 150(13) = 2,130.

A club needs to raise *at least* $500 and has $124 so far. It sells candles for $8 each. Let c be the number of candles: 124 + 8c ≥ 500. Subtract 124: 8c ≥ 376. Divide by 8: c ≥ 47. They must sell 47 or more candles. Check: 124 + 8(47) = 124 + 376 = 500 exactly, so 47 just reaches the goal and 46 falls short at 492.

Translate the phrases carefully. 'At most 30' and 'no more than 30' both mean ≤ 30. 'At least 30' and 'no fewer than 30' both mean ≥ 30. 'More than 30' is strictly > 30. After solving, decide which numbers are actually *feasible*: whole numbers for people or candles, and never negative. A model with a solution like p ≤ 12.13 is telling you 12, not 12.13, and not 13.

words.d: a limit the situation places on the variable, such as a weight capacity
no more than; translates to ≤
no fewer than; translates to ≥
a value that is allowed by every constraint and makes sense in the situation

look.title: Loading the Truck
look.text: A pickup can carry at most 1,200 pounds. It already holds 300 pounds of tools. Bags of soil weigh 40 pounds each. Let b be the number of bags: 300 + 40b ≤ 1200. Subtract 300: 40b ≤ 900. Divide by 40: b ≤ 22.5. Since half a bag is not sold, the truck can take 22 bags. Check: 300 + 40(22) = 1,180, under the limit.
look.prompt: If the tools are unloaded first, how many bags fit? Write and solve the new inequality.

check.q: Which inequality means 'no more than 30 people'?
check.why: 'No more than 30' allows 30 itself and anything smaller, which is x ≤ 30.

check.q: A club has $124 and sells candles for $8 each. How many must it sell to reach at least $500?
check.why: 124 + 8c ≥ 500 gives 8c ≥ 376 and c ≥ 47. Selling 46 gives only $492. Dividing 500 by 8 ignores the $124 already raised.

check.q: An elevator holds 2,000 pounds. A 180-pound cart is inside and workers average 150 pounds. How many workers can ride?
check.why: 180 + 150p ≤ 2000 gives p ≤ 12.13, so 12 workers. Thirteen would total 2,130 pounds, over the limit.

lessons.title: Units and Reasonableness
lessons.mainIdea: Carry the units through your work and compare the answer to a rough estimate before you trust it.
reading: Back to the fertilizer bag: 3 pounds for every 1,000 square feet. A bed 40 feet by 60 feet has area 40 ft × 60 ft = 2,400 square feet. The rate is 3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, so pounds = 2,400 sq ft × (3 lb / 1,000 sq ft) = 7.2 lb. Notice the square feet cancel and only pounds remain. This tracking of units is called *unit analysis*. If a student multiplied by 3 without dividing by 1,000, the answer would be 7,200, and the leftover units would be pound-square-feet, which is meaningless. The units flag the error.

An *estimate* catches errors too. Before computing, ask: is 2,400 square feet more or less than 1,000? It is a bit more than double, so the answer should be a bit more than double 3 pounds, roughly 6 to 8. An answer of 7.2 is *reasonable*; an answer of 720 or 0.72 is not. Estimating first takes ten seconds and saves a whole wrong page.

Time is the unit that trips people up most. A trip of 60 miles at 40 miles per hour takes 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 hours. That is 1 hour and 30 minutes, not 1 hour and 50 minutes, because 0.5 hour × 60 minutes per hour = 30 minutes. Likewise 0.6 hour is 36 minutes. And some answers are impossible on their face: −3 tickets, 4.5 people, or a 90-year-old kindergartner. When the number is impossible, the model or the arithmetic is wrong, not the world.

words.d: tracking units through a calculation and canceling them like factors
a rough answer found quickly, used to judge whether the exact answer makes sense
an answer whose size and units fit the situation

look.title: Fertilizer for Different Beds
look.cite: example rate of 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet, a typical instruction on lawn fertilizer bags
look.prompt: Doubling the area doubles the pounds. Use the table to estimate the pounds for 3,300 square feet before you calculate it exactly.

check.q: How many minutes is 0.6 hour?
check.why: 0.6 × 60 minutes = 36 minutes. Reading 0.6 hour as '60 minutes' or as '6 minutes' is a common slip.

check.q: A bed is 30 feet by 50 feet. At 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet, how much fertilizer is needed?
check.why: Area is 30 × 50 = 1,500 sq ft, which is 1.5 thousands, so 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 pounds. An answer of 4,500 forgot to divide by 1,000.

check.q: Which answer should make you recheck your work?
check.why: A negative number of tickets is impossible, so either the equation or the arithmetic has an error. The other answers are all plausible.

review.q: Which value is a solution of 6x − 5 = 31?

review.why: Distribute: 2x − 8 = 3x − 15. Subtract 2x: −8 = x − 15. Add 15: x = 7. Check: 2(3) = 6 and 21 − 15 = 6.
r is multiplied by 2π, so divide both sides by 2π: r = C/(2π).
x − 5 = 2 gives 7; x − 5 = −2 gives 3. Both numbers are 2 units from 5.
Subtract 7: −2x > −6. Divide by −2 and reverse: x < 3. Check x = 0: 7 > 1 is true.
Subtract 1 from all parts: 2 ≤ 2x ≤ 10. Divide by 2: 1 ≤ x ≤ 5.

review.q: A plumber charges $60 to visit plus $45 per hour. The bill is $240. How many hours did the job take?
review.why: 60 + 45h = 240, so 45h = 180 and h = 4. Dividing 240 by 45 ignores the visit fee.

review.q: A van seats at most 12 people. Two adults must ride. Which inequality gives the number of students s?
review.why: The two adults plus the students cannot exceed 12 seats: 2 + s ≤ 12, so s ≤ 10.
